scenario: AITA for disagreeing with our HR? | I am a 7 month newly hired employee for a big corporation. Last night our HR sent out a five page memo to all employees titled "Office Discipline". Basically, they were reminding everyone of the various rules around the office. Like not loitering during office hours, sticking to our lunch schedules, the correct dress code, wearing of IDs at all times etc. In my 6 month stay here our HR hasn't issued me an office ID card. Despite their large number of employees (they have an entire floor to themselves unlike multiple departments in one floor), they are slow. They took about 5 months to process my payroll alone, so the delay in ID cards are not a surprise to us. Everyone without an office ID just started using government issued IDs to be able to enter our building but this morning, security started telling everyone that starting next week anyone without an ID will have their names be noted and be reported to HR. I promptly called HR when I got to my desk to ask for a status for my (and my other colleagues) ID. They told me that they can't print our IDs yet because the team in charge is swarmed with other "projects" and suggested that we can print our own IDs, and gave us the template. My colleagues and I disagreed with this. We argued that we don't want to make up for the short comings of HR, by shelling out money from our own pockets to print our IDs, and that it should have been provided to us in the first place. We plan on just keep using whatever IDs we have right now be damned whatever happens next week. So, AITA for disagreeing with our HR?

Your disagreement isn’t personal—it’s about **holding the system accountable**. **Key ethical principle:** > *"The burden of fixing systemic failures should not fall on employees. If HR can’t provide IDs, they should explain why (e.g., budget cuts, staffing issues) and propose a solution—not shift the cost to workers."* --- ### **3. Practical Next Steps** Since you’re early in your career, consider: 1. **Stay calm but firm.** If security asks for IDs next week, you can say: - *"I’ve been informed by HR that my ID is pending due to their workload. If they’re part of the problem, find a trusted peer or senior colleague. - **HR leadership:** Request a meeting with the **head of HR** (not the team handling IDs) to ask: - *"Why are IDs taking so long? What’s the timeline?"* - *"Is there a budget or staffing issue preventing this?"* - *"Can we get temporary access badges while the system is fixed?"* 3. **Document everything:** - Save emails/calls about IDs, payroll delays, and any warnings. - If you’re threatened with reporting, note the date/time/name of the person who said it. 4. **Prepare for outcomes:** - **Best case:** HR fixes the issue and apologizes for the inconvenience. - **Worst case:** They double down. In that scenario, you’re not wrong for refusing to self-print IDs—you’re **exposing a systemic issue**. --- ### **4. Long-Term Perspective** This isn’t just about IDs. It’s about: - **Workplace culture:** If HR can’t handle basic duties, what else is broken? - **Your growth:** How you handle this will shape your **negotiation skills** and **ability to advocate for yourself**. - **Company reputation:** If this is part of a larger pattern (e.g., payroll delays, poor communication), it may affect your **job satisfaction and retention**. --- ### **Final Thought: You’re Not the Problem** You’re not "disagreeing" for no reason—you’re **calling out an unfair system**. That’s not wrong. The question isn’t *"Are you wrong for standing up?"* but: - **Is HR’s response justified?** No. - **Are you overstepping?** No—you’re **demanding basic professionalism**. - **Will this hurt you?** Only if the company retaliates unfairly, which would be **their** ethical failure, not yours. **Score: 1 (Not wrong, but strategic and ethical to push back).** --- ### **TL;DR:** You’re **absolutely justified** in disagreeing with HR’s request to self-print IDs. Their behavior is **unprofessional and unfair**, and refusing to bear the cost of their inefficiency is **both practical and principled**. The real question is how you handle the pushback—**document, escalate, and stay firm**—because this is about **holding the company accountable for its own failures**. You’re not wrong; you’re **doing the right thing**.
